newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Leghold trap debate to top EU foreign ministers talks.
newsitem.headline: Leghold trap debate to top EU foreign ministers talks.

text.p: Luxembourg will make a new bid next week to get the European Union to agree a deal with Canada and Russia on humane standards for leg-hold traps, but EU officials say it is likely to be blocked again.

Foreign Ministers meeting at the General Affairs Council on Tuesday will tackle leg-hold traps, the Commission's Agenda 2000 enlargement plans, Middle East peace, a trade agreement with Jordan and the situation in former Yugoslavia and Albania.
"It is a pretty routine agenda, but the leg-hold trap issue is one that could go either way," said an EU official.
The EU has been at odds with Canada, Russia and the United States for years over differences regarding what constitutes a humane way of trapping and killing fur-bearing animals.
The 15-nation bloc passed a law in 1991 making it illegal from January 1995 for the EU to import any fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps or so-called "drowning traps".

The law was postponed for a year but has still never been implemented as the Commission -- the EU's executive -- persuaded member states that they face a serious risk of World Trade Organisation action if they banned imports of trapped fur.
The European Parliament and some member states such as Britain, however, have been arguing for a stronger stance and are furious with what they see as delaying tactics by the Commission.
On Tuesday Luxembourg -- the current EU president -- will introduce a proposal by which the EU would agree to allow imports of fur from animals caught in traps that met agreed humane standards.
Luxembourg hopes such a deal will pressure the U.S. into also coming on board, but Britain and France have been suggesting they will oppose the move.

Russia, Canada and the U.S. argue that trapping fur is a legitimate way of life for thousands of indigenous ethnic groups and a ban on their products is unacceptable extra-territorial trade legislation.
The foreign ministers meeting will open with a traditional beginning of presidency debate during which Agenda 2000 -- the EU's enlargement plans -- is likely to feature.

Foreign Ministers have also invited their Israeli counterpart, David Levy, for a dinner meeting and EU sources say Luxembourg officials are currently trying to persuade Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to attend as well.
Ministers will also discuss the situation in former Yugoslavia as well as an international donors conference on Bosnian reconstruction to be held in Brussels on Wednesday and Thursday.

Foreign ministers from the Western European Union -- a fledgling defence and political union incorporating the EU's states as either members or observers and including Turkey, Norway and Iceland -- will also meet on Tuesday to add a symbolic note to the Treaty of Amsterdam.
